sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: SKYROCKET is a single-center, single-arm phase II study that evaluated whether the addition of stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) to atezolizumab plus tiragolumab enhances antitumor efficacy in PD-L1–positive non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: Patients received SBRT to all metastatic sites and subsequently received atezolizumab and tiragolumab every 3 weeks on day 1 of each 21-day cycle with 7 days of completion of SBRT. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed progression-free survival (PFS) from the start of SBRT. Exploratory endpoints included single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) obtained from tumor biopsies at baseline (BL) and on-treatment (OT) and were further characterized as clinical benefit [CB; partial response or stable disease (SD) ≥ 6 months] and non–clinical benefit (NCB; progressive disease or SD < 6 months).

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Forty-one patients were enrolled. At a median duration of follow-up of 9.8 months, median PFS at the start of SBRT was 9.3 months [95% confidence interval (CI), 6.0–NR]. No new safety signal was observed. scRNA-seq of paired BL and OT (n = 3) and single–time point (n = 2) revealed that CD8 progenitor-exhausted (TPEX) cells markedly expanded after treatment, with high T-cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM (TIGIT) and PD-1 expression in CD8 TPEX/TEX subsets. CD4 regulatory T cells (Treg) were reduced in the CB group but increased in the NCB group. The CB group showed reduced Treg suppression and NECTIN–TIGIT signaling, whereas NCB maintained proliferative CTLA4high/TIGIThigh Treg supported by ICAM/galectin–CTLA4 pathways.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: SBRT followed by atezolizumab plus tiragolumab showed encouraging clinical activity with manageable safety in PD-L1–positive metastatic NSCLC.
Received 2026 Jan 1; Revised 2026 Feb 19; Accepted 2026 Apr 13; Issue date 2026 Jul 17.

boxed-text.p: In PD-L1–positive metastatic non–small cell lung cancer, atezolizumab plus tiragolumab after stereotactic body radiotherapy improves progression-free survival with a manageable safety profile. Combination therapy boosts cytotoxic/helper T-cell programs in clinical benefit, whereas persistent ICAM/galectin–CTLA4-driven regulatory T cells underlie resistance to treatment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) including programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors as monotherapy or combination have revolutionized the treatment landscape for metastatic non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without driver alterations (1). Despite the clinical benefit and durable antitumor response in a subset of patients, there is still an unmet need in patients who do not initially respond to immunotherapy. To overcome resistance mechanisms to immunotherapies (2), various strategies are ongoing such as the development of ivonescimab, a bispecific antibody targeting both PD-1 and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which showed improvement in progression-free survival (PFS) in previously untreated PD-L1–positive, advanced NSCLC (3). Other ongoing efforts include targeting other immune checkpoint molecules such as T-cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM (TIGIT), which binds with its ligand PVR to inhibit T-cell activation (4). Inhibition of TIGIT along with the PD-1/PD-L1 axis has been shown to augment antitumor response in murine models (5). Tiragolumab, an anti-TIGIT antibody, improves PD-L1 blockade through modulation of myeloid and regulatory T cells (Treg) in the tumor microenvironment (TME; ref. 6).

Oligometastatic disease in NSCLC is relatively indolent in terms of progression compared with bulky, symptomatic disease and allows for local treatment, including radiotherapy (7). Radiotherapy and immunotherapy have complementary effects: radiotherapy reduces tumor burden and potentiates the local effect of immunotherapy by modulating the TME through increased T-cell infiltration into tumors. Immunotherapy enhances radiotherapy-induced immune activation, blocks radiotherapy-induced PD-L1 upregulation, and eliminates microscopic disease. Two prospective trials of pembrolizumab with or without local ablative therapy, including stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) in NSCLC have demonstrated the feasibility and safety of adding SBRT to immunotherapy (8, 9). Although the addition of SBRT to all metastatic sites showed an improvement of PFS of approximately 12 months (9), SBRT to only one metastatic site did not result in improvement of objective response rate (ORR), PFS, or overall survival (OS; ref. 8).

Atezolizumab is a PD-L1 inhibitor approved in resected stages II–IIIA NSCLC (10) and as monotherapy in previously untreated metastatic NSCLC with high PD-L1 expression (11). Previously, the phase II CITYSCAPE demonstrated improvement in ORR and PFS in patients treated with first-line tiragolumab plus atezolizumab compared with atezolizumab in PD-L1–positive NSCLC with a greater magnitude of benefit in tumor proportion score (TPS) ≥ 50% (12). However, the subsequent phase III SKYSCRAPER-01 study failed to show an improvement in OS in PD-L1–high, previously untreated metastatic NSCLC (13). Before the publication of these results, we conducted SKYROCKET, a single-arm phase II trial of atezolizumab plus tiragolumab after completion of SBRT as first-line therapy in PD-L1–selected metastatic NSCLC without driver alterations to evaluate the antitumor activity of this combination.

Variability in tiragolumab efficacy across clinical studies indicates that the immunologic basis of response to TIGIT blockade remains incompletely understood (12, 13). TIGIT is a central coinhibitory receptor expressed on exhausted CD8+ T cells, Treg, and NK cells. Its engagement with the PVR–NECTIN axis shapes multiple dimensions of the tumor-immune microenvironment (14, 15). Therefore, in this study, we aimed not only to evaluate the antitumor activity of tiragolumab in combination with atezolizumab plus SBRT but also to delineate its potential novel mechanisms of action at the transcriptomic level.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: SKYROCKET is a single-center, single-arm phase II nonrandomized controlled trial that enrolled treatment-naïve patients diagnosed with metastatic NSCLC amenable to SBRT and who were positive for PD-L1 expression and negative for EGFR, ALK, and ROS1. Positive PD-L1 expression was defined as TPS ≥ 1% using immunohistochemistry (IHC) 22C3 pharmDx assay (Dako, Agilent Technologies). Key exclusion criteria included double primary lung cancers, lesions that were not amenable to radiotherapy, including pleural effusion, peritoneal seeding, or leptomeningeal meningeal metastasis. Multiple lesions that result in radiotherapy dose beyond normal organ dose were also excluded from the study.

Enrolled patients first received SBRT within 26 days after informed consent and were treated with atezolizumab plus tiragolumab within 7 days after SBRT. This trial was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Yonsei Cancer Center (4-2021-0891) and was conducted according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided written informed consent at the time of enrollment.

sec.title: Radiotherapy
sec.p: Two independent radiologists determined whether SBRT was amenable using the following principles: (i) ideally irradiate the majority of lesions (minimum of 1 and maximum of 10 lesions to be irradiated); (ii) select FDG avid lesion or lesions that are showing active growth in the PET scan that was completed within 56 days before radiotherapy; (iii) dose constraints may not be exceeded, and if there is an overlap of the target with an organ at risk, the dose can be reduced, the number of fractions can be increased, or the target coverage compromised to meet the constraint; (iv) lesions that have been treated with radiotherapy within the last 6 months will not be radiated; and (v) the number of allowable doses and fractionations are as follows: for one, two, and three fractions, the preferred dose and acceptable doses are 20 Gy (16–24 Gy), 30 Gy (24–33 Gy), and 35 Gy (25–40 Gy), respectively.

sec.title: Treatment with atezolizumab and tiragolumab
sec.p: After completion of SBRT, all patients subsequently received a fixed intravenous dose of 1,200 mg of atezolizumab and 600 mg of tiragolumab every 3 weeks on day 1 of each 21-day cycle in alignment with the phase II CITYSCAPE study (16). Dose reduction was not permitted for either atezolizumab or tiragolumab.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: The primary endpoint of this study was investigator-assessed PFS from the start of SBRT using RECIST v.1.1. Secondary endpoints were PFS by PD-L1 expression high (PD-L1 of 50% or more), OS, and safety as per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events criteria. CT, brain MRI, and PET-CT scans were performed at baseline, and patients were followed up with CT scans every 12 weeks until investigator-assessed disease progression. Upon treatment discontinuation, patients were monitored for survival every 6 months until follow-up loss, consent withdrawal, or death, and 6 weeks after the last dose for adverse events (AE).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The sample size was calculated based on the following design. Assuming a power of 80%, a type I error of 10%, and a 10% dropout rate, 45 patients were required for accrual.

PFS was analyzed in the full analysis population and was defined as the time from starting treatment with atezolizumab plus tiragolumab to progression to disease or death due to any cause. OS was defined as the time from starting treatment to death due to any cause. The Cox proportional hazards model was used to calculate the hazard ratio (HR), and baseline demographics and treatment-related AE (TRAE) were compared using the χ2 test. All analyses were performed using R v4.3.3 and SAS v9.4. The swimmer plot was visualized using dplyr (RRID: SCR_016708) and ggplot2 (RRID: SCR_014601) in R.

sec.title: Exploratory analysis
sec.p: As part of the exploratory analysis, baseline tissue samples were mandatory, and rebiopsy after C2/progressive disease (PD) was optional. Further analysis was done using multiplexed biomarker analysis and gene expression profile and immune cell marker via single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq).

sec.title: scRNA-seq preprocessing and quality control
sec.p: Fresh-frozen tumor tissues were dissociated and processed for scRNA-seq using the 10x Genomics Chromium Single Cell 5′ kit (10x Genomics, 5′ end chromium, RRID: SCR_019326). Library construction and sequencing were performed by Macrogen Inc. After cDNA quality assessment, sequencing depth was determined based on the number of detected cells and the quality metrics of the libraries. When the initial unique molecular identifier counts and read depth were found to be insufficient, additional sequencing was conducted to achieve optimal coverage. The raw sequencing data were processed using Cell Ranger (version 7.0.1, 10x Genomics, RRID: SCR_017344) with the prebuilt GRCh38 human reference transcriptome. Downstream analyses were performed using the Seurat R package (version 5.1.0, RRID: SCR_016341; ref. 17). Cells were retained if they exhibited > 90% human gene content, < 20% mitochondrial gene abundance, and expression of at least 100 genes. Genes expressed in fewer than three cells were excluded. Doublets were detected and removed using the DoubletFinder algorithm (v2.0.3, RRID: SCR_018771; ref. 18). Cell-type annotation was performed based on canonical lineage marker expression, including PTPRC, CD3D, CD79A, LYZ, VWF, and COL1A1, among others. All specimens were pathologically confirmed as tumor lesions before downstream molecular analyses, and multiplex IHC (mIHC) was performed on representative tumor sections to validate the presence and spatial distribution of tumor and immune cell populations (Supplementary Fig. S1).

sec.title: Differential gene expression and pathway analysis
sec.p: Differentially expressed genes (DEG) between clusters or clinical groups were identified using the FindMarkers function implemented in Seurat (version 5.1.0, RRID: SCR_016341; ref. 17). Genes were defined as differentially expressed when the log fold change exceeded 0.15 and when they were expressed in at least 15% of cells in both groups. Gene Ontology (GO) term enrichment analyses were performed using the clusterProfiler R package (v4.12.6, RRID: SCR_016884; ref. 19), and the results were visualized with the enrichGO function within the same package. Signature scores for selected gene sets were calculated using the AddModuleScore function implemented in Seurat (version 5.1.0, RRID: SCR_016341; ref. 17).

sec.title: Trajectory analysis of scRNA-seq
sec.p: Developmental trajectories of the cells were inferred using Monocle 3 (v1.3.7, RRID: SCR_018685; ref. 20). T-cell subsets were first extracted from the Seurat object. The learn_graph function in Monocle3 was then applied to construct the principal trajectory graph within each partition. Cells were subsequently ordered along a pseudotime axis by computing the shortest paths through the learned graph. Naïve T cells (TN) were designated as root nodes to anchor the trajectory inference. We used Slingshot (v2.12.0, RRID: SCR_017012; ref. 21) to infer pseudotime trajectories of T cells within the TME. To identify DEG between terminally differentiated states across lineages, we applied the diffEnd function from tradeSeq (v1.18.0, RRID: SCR_019238; ref. 22). The resulting DEG sets were subjected to pathway enrichment analysis using the enrichGO function in clusterProfiler (v4.12.6, RRID: SCR_016884; ref. 19), referencing the Reactome and GO Biological Process (GO:BP) gene sets. Only pathways with adjusted P values < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

sec.title: Prediction of cell-to-cell interactions in scRNA-seq data
sec.p: Cell–cell interactions among immune cell subsets were inferred from scRNA-seq data using the CellChat R package (v2.1.2, RRID: SCR_021946; ref. 23). Analyses were performed with default parameters, and interactions involving fewer than 10 cells per group were excluded to ensure statistical robustness. Statistically significant interactions (P < 0.05) were retained, and subsequent analyses focused on biologically relevant signaling pathways mediating communication between immune cell subpopulations across clinical groups.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using R (v4.4.2). Continuous variables between two groups were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, as appropriate. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05; *, P < 0.01; and **, P < 0.001.

sec.title: Patient population
sec.p: Patients were recruited between July 21, 2022, and January 13, 2025, at Yonsei Cancer Center. Of 53 patients assessed for eligibility, 45 eligible patients were enrolled. A total of 41 Asian patients received SBRT followed by atezolizumab plus tiragolumab (Supplementary Fig. S2). The median age was 70 years (range, 50–88 years), and most patients were current (n = 18, 44%) and former (n = 18, 44%) smokers (Table 1). Adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma accounted for 51% (n = 21) and 49% (n = 20), respectively. Twenty-five (56%) patients had PD-L1 expression of 1 to 49, and 16 (39%) patients had PD-L1 expression of 50% or more. All patients had more than one site of metastasis, and the most common site of metastasis was bone (n = 13, 32%) and contralateral lung (n = 10, 24%). The representativeness of the study population with respect to key demographic and clinical characteristics is summarized in Supplementary Table S1.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: The cutoff date was August 1, 2025, and the median follow-up was 9.8 months (IQR, 6.3–15.8). The median treated cycles were 9 (range, 2–51). The median treatment duration was 6 months [95% confidence interval (CI), 5–8 months]. At the time of analysis, 15 (37%) patients were receiving treatment. The median PFS at the start of SBRT was 9.3 months (95% CI, CI 6–not evaluable; Fig. 1A). The median OS was immature at the time of analysis with 26 (63%) patients who discontinued treatment and 18 (44%) patients died (Fig. 1B). The most common reason of treatment discontinuation was due to disease progression (n = 18, 63%; Supplementary Fig. S2).

caption.p: A, PFS from the start of SBRT, B, OS from the start of SBRT, C, PFS by PD-L1 expression, D, OS by PD-L1 expression from the start of SBRT, and E, swimmer plot. Abbreviations: NE, not evaluable; PR, partial response.

sec.p: Further analysis by PD-L1 expression showed that PFS benefit was observed in patients with high PD-L1 (≥ 50%) expression with a median PFS of 11.4 versus 6.4 months (P = 0.029, HR, 0.39, 95% CI, 0.16–0.95) in patients with low PD-L1 (< 50%) expression (Fig. 1C). The median OS was not reached in patients with PD-L1 ≥ 50% because of immature follow-up, compared with 9.2 months in those with PD-L1 < 50% (P = 0.007; HR, 0.22; 95% CI, 0.09–0.55; Fig. 1D). The benefit of SBRT plus atezolizumab with tiragolumab translated into OS in the PD-L1–high subset (not reached) versus PD-L1–low subset (9.2 months; P = 0.007; HR, 0.22; 95% CI, 0.09–0.55). The median PFS and OS from the start of atezolizumab plus tiragolumab were comparable with the results at the start of SBRT (Supplementary Fig. S3).

Of the 41 treated patients, 39 patients had measurable lesions (Fig. 1E). Nineteen patients (46%) experienced disease progression. The most common pattern of relapse was progression at the original site (n = 11, 27%), followed by involvement of both the original and new sites (n = 5, 12%) and new metastatic sites only (n = 3, 7%).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Overall, SBRT followed by atezolizumab plus tiragolumab was safe and well tolerated. TRAE due to SBRT occurred in 12 (29%) patients. The most common AE were grades 1 and 2 esophagitis (n = 9, 22%), followed by radiation pneumonitis (n = 3, 7%) and pneumonia (n = 1, 2%). None of the patients experienced grade 3 TRAE from SBRT (Table 2). TRAE due to atezolizumab plus tiragolumab occurred in 29 (71%) patients. Most of the AE were of grades 1 and 2. Urticaria (n = 19, 46%) was the most common AE, followed by skin rash (n = 8, 20%), increased alanine transaminase (n = 8, 20%), and aspartate transaminase (n = 7, 17%). Pneumonitis occurred in two (5%) patients; one patient experienced grade 3 pneumonitis. TRAE due to atezolizumab plus tiragolumab, resulting in dose interruption and permanent discontinuation, occurred in five (12%) and two (5%) patients, respectively. TRAE due to SBRT occurred in 12 (29%) patients. The most common AE were grades 1 and 2 esophagitis (n = 9, 22%), followed by radiation pneumonitis (n = 3, 7%) and pneumonia (n = 1, 2%). None of the patients experienced grade 3 TRAE from SBRT.

sec.title: CD8 T-cell dynamics and functional remodeling following tiragolumab plus atezolizumab therapy
sec.p: To elucidate the mechanistic impact of combination therapy, we performed scRNA-seq on biopsied samples from five patients. This included a total of eight tissue samples: four baseline (BL) samples collected before irradiation and four on-treatment (OT) samples obtained at cycle 2 day 1 (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Table S2). BL samples included soft tissue mass around the rib (n = 1) and mediastinal lymph nodes (LN) (n = 3). OT samples included the lung (n = 1), mediastinal LN (n = 2), and soft tissue mass around the rib (n = 1). Among these patients, three patients had paired biopsied samples. Based on canonical lineage markers, eight major clusters were identified, which were further segregated in Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction space according to sampling time point and clinical response (Supplementary Fig. S4). Compared with BL samples, OT samples displayed an increased abundance of NK/T-cell clusters (Supplementary Fig. S5A and S5B).

Three patients provided paired BL and OT samples, and two patients contributed single–time point biopsies (four BL and four OT samples in total). sec.p: Focusing on CD8+ T cells, subclustering analysis revealed seven transcriptionally distinct subsets characterized by representative marker genes (Fig. 2B; Supplementary Fig. S5C and S5D). Notably, the progenitor-exhausted CD8 T cells (TPEX), previously associated with ICI responsiveness (24, 25), showed a significant expansion after therapy (Fig. 2C). Differential expression analysis between BL and OT samples indicated enrichment of “cellular response to radiation” and “antigen receptor–mediated signaling” pathways during OT CD8 T cells (Fig. 2D). Among the subsets, the radiation-response score was the highest in CD8 TPEX and residential-memory CD8 T cells (TRM; Fig. 2E). Interestingly, this score was more pronounced in the non–clinical benefit [NCB; PD + stable disease (SD) < 6 months] group than in the clinical benefit (CB; partial response + SD ≥ 6 months) group, suggesting that radiation-associated responses might negatively influence immunoradiation therapeutic outcome (Fig. 2E; Supplementary Fig. S5E).

To evaluate target engagement, expression of TIGIT and PDCD1, the targets of tiragolumab and atezolizumab, was the highest in exhausted CD8 T-cell (TEX) and TPEX subsets (Fig. 2F). Functional pathway analysis of DEG showed that OT samples were enriched in T-cell activation and T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling pathways, whereas negative regulators such as NF-κB transduction and leukocyte cytotoxicity pathways were downregulated (Fig. 2G and H; Supplementary Fig. S5F and S5G). Consistent with this finding, the cytotoxicity score (GZMA, GZMB, GZMK, GNLY, IFNG, PRF1, and NKG7) increased following treatment in the CB group but decreased in NCB samples (Fig. 2I). Notably, CD8 TPEX increased in both groups after therapy. In contrast, CD8 TEX expanded following treatment in the CB group but decreased in NCB patients (Supplementary Fig. S5H). Trajectory inference further revealed a shift in differentiation from effector-memory CD8 T cells (TEM) to TPEX and TEX cells after therapy, whereas BL samples predominantly followed a TEM → TRM pathway (Fig. 2J). TRADEseq analysis identified a downregulation of type I IFN production and NO biosynthetic processes, concomitant with upregulation of T-cell migration and innate immune-activation pathways during OT samples (Fig. 2K).

Collectively, these data suggest that tiragolumab plus atezolizumab therapy selectively enhances activation and expansion of CD8 TEX and TPEX subsets via cross-talk with innate immune cells, thereby reinforcing adaptive immune responses in clinically beneficial cases.

sec.title: CD4 T-cell remodeling and Treg suppression dynamics following tiragolumab plus atezolizumab therapy
sec.p: To further delineate the role of CD4 T cells in the TME during treatment, we performed subclustering analysis on CD4 T cells and identified six transcriptionally distinct subsets, including CD4 TN, CD4 CXCL13+, CD4 IL7+, central-memory T cells (TCM), TEM, and Treg populations (Fig. 3A; Supplementary Fig. S6A and S6B). Notably, the proportions of CD4 CXCL13+ and Treg populations showed distinct trends according to clinical outcome. CD4 CXCL13+ T cells markedly increased in the CB group after therapy, whereas no significant change was observed in the NCB group. In contrast, Treg decreased following treatment in the CB group but expanded in NCB patients (Fig. 3B). These reciprocal dynamics suggest that therapeutic efficacy is associated with enhanced helper-type differentiation and concurrent attenuation of Treg activity.

caption.p: Single-cell analysis of CD4 T cells and trajectories. A, UMAP visualization of intratumoral CD4 T cells. B, Relative proportions (%) of CD4 CXCL13 and CD4 Treg at BL and OT in CB and NCB patients, shown as box plots. C, Dot plot of TIGIT and PDCD1 expression in intratumoral CD4 T-cell subtypes at BL. D, Distinct differentiation trajectories of CD4+ T cells between BL and OT at CB and NCB. Lineage relationships were mapped from progenitor states to terminal states. E and F, TRADEseq analysis of CD4 T-cell trajectories in CB and NCB. G, GO biological process enrichment (enrichGO, P < 0.05) of upregulated genes in CD4 Treg cells at NCB and CB at OT. H, CD4 Treg suppression scores displayed as violin plots for BL versus OT (left) and within OT samples by clinical benefit (NCB vs. CB; right). P values were calculated using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. I, Violin plots display the dynamics of tumor suppression–related genes in response to treatment.

sec.p: Expression profiling of immune checkpoints revealed that TIGIT and PDCD1 were predominantly expressed in Treg and CD4 CXCL13+ subsets at BL (Fig. 3C), suggesting potential engagement of these cell types by tiragolumab plus atezolizumab. Pseudotime trajectory analysis demonstrated that CD4 TEM cells in CB samples predominantly differentiated into the CD4 CXCL13+ lineage following treatment, whereas those in NCB samples were largely biased toward a Treg lineage (Fig. 3D). TRADEseq-based pathway analysis revealed that in the CB group, the TEM → CXCL13+ T transition was associated with activation of inflammasome signaling, type I IFN responses, and PRR-mediated innate signaling, whereas the TEM → Treg transition involved TGFβ receptor signaling and IL10 production (Fig. 3E). In contrast, NCB samples displayed enrichment of leukocyte migration and receptor recycling pathways, along with attenuated IFNβ signaling (Fig. 3F), implying impaired helper to effector conversion and sustained immunoregulatory dominance.

We next investigated the transcriptional dynamics of Treg, which exhibited distinct signatures between CB and NCB groups. Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that OT samples from CB patients upregulated genes related to dendritic cell (DC) chemotaxis, TCR signaling, and cytokine responses to IFNβ, indicating a functionally activated yet less-suppressive regulatory phenotype. In contrast, Treg from NCB samples were enriched in pathways associated with inflammatory responses, lymphocyte proliferation, mononuclear cell expansion, and cytokine responses to TNF, consistent with a persistently suppressive and proliferative Treg state (Fig. 3G). Consistently, suppression scores (FOXP3, CTLA4, CCL8, TNFRSF1B, TNFRSF8, IL10, TNFRSF4, TNFRSF9, and TNFRSF18) were significantly reduced from BL to OT in the Treg and remained markedly lower in CB than in NCB samples at OT (Fig. 3H and I).

Collectively, these findings suggest that in responders, tiragolumab plus atezolizumab therapy alleviates BL Treg dominance and promotes immune remodeling toward a balanced helper response. In contrast, nonresponders exhibit enhanced differentiation toward the Treg lineage, improving regulatory predominance and diminished IFN-induced signaling. Effective therapeutic response is therefore characterized by coordinated activation of helper T-cell programs accompanied by attenuation of suppressive Treg activity.

sec.title: SBRT induces stromal remodeling through ECM-associated activation of myeloid cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts
sec.p: Subsequently, myeloid cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) were identified to further characterize the nonlymphoid components of the TME. Myeloid cells were classified into nine distinct clusters based on representative marker genes, including CXCL10+, SPP1+, FOLR2+, and TREM2+ macrophages, as well as extracellular matrix–remodeling tumor-associated macrophages (ECM-remodeling TAM) and DC subsets (cDC1 and cDC2; Supplementary Fig. S7A and S7B). Although no statistically significant difference in overall myeloid abundance was observed between BL and OT, a trend toward increased ECM-remodeling TAM was detected (Supplementary Fig. S7C). To assess the therapeutic impact on myeloid compartments, differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed between BL and OT samples (Supplementary Fig. S7D and S7E). Notably, COL1A1 and COL1A2 were significantly upregulated during OT samples, accompanied by enrichment of the “response to radiation” pathway. Moreover, comparison of pathway scores revealed that ECM-remodeling TAM exhibited dominant expression of these signatures, with higher levels observed in the CB group (Supplementary Fig. S7F and S7G). These findings suggest that SBRT induces the emergence of ECM-remodeling TAM, thereby promoting to stromal reorganization within the TME.

CAF were identified and classified into six distinct clusters based on canonical marker genes (Supplementary Fig. S8A and S8B). Among these, the ECM-CAF population significantly increased during OT samples, whereas CD86+ antigen-presenting CAF (CD86+ apCAF) were markedly decreased (Supplementary Fig. S8C). To assess the therapeutic effects on total CAF compartments, differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed between BL and OT samples (Supplementary Fig. S8D and S8E). Interestingly, similar to the myeloid compartment, COL1A1 and COL1A2 were significantly upregulated during OT samples, accompanied by activation of the “response to UV” pathway. Moreover, comparison of pathway scores indicated that ECM-CAF clusters dominantly expressed these ECM-related signatures, with higher levels observed in the CB group (Supplementary Fig. S8F and S8G). These findings suggest that SBRT activates ECM-organization pathways within CAF, thereby promoting structural remodeling of the TME.

sec.title: Attenuation of NECTIN–TIGIT signaling associates with Treg restraint and clinical benefit
sec.p: TIGIT binds PVR (CD155) and NECTIN2 (CD112), whereas PD-1 binds PD-L1 (CD274; ref. 26). Among ligands, NECTIN2 showed the strongest expression, with peak levels in CXCL10+ macrophages, cDC2, and CD86+ apCAF (Supplementary Fig. S9A). Compositionally, the CB group exhibited reduced frequencies of CXCL10+ macrophages and cDC2 after therapy, whereas NCB samples showed minimal change (Supplementary Fig. S9B). Therefore, we next tested whether the decline of NECTIN2-high sender populations in CB translated into weaker NECTIN–TIGIT signaling. CellChat analysis of OT samples revealed that the overall quantity and strength of NECTIN interactions were lower in CB than in NCB, with NECTIN2–TIGIT and NECTIN3–TIGIT pairs showing significant reductions (Supplementary Fig. S9C and S9D). Mapping receptors and ligands across compartments confirmed that T-lymphoid clusters, particularly Treg, were the dominant receivers, whereas NECTIN ligands were concentrated in nonlymphoid senders (CXCL10+ macrophages, cDC2, and apCAF; Supplementary Fig. S9E). Together, the data indicate that therapeutic attenuation of NECTIN–TIGIT signaling reduces Treg-mediated suppression, thereby increasing the probability of clinical benefit.

sec.title: Failure of Treg suppression in NCB: ICAM/galectin-driven CD4 TEM recruitment and CTLA4high suppressive Treg promotion
sec.p: We next investigated why Treg suppression fails in NCB despite therapy, delineating mechanisms that sustain TIGIT-driven regulation. Pseudotime analysis of Treg-specific programs revealed that the CD4 TEM → Treg transition score increased in NCB but not in CB during the CD4 TEM status (Fig. 4A). To assess specific changes during the CD4 TEM phase along pseudotime, we performed a signaling pattern analysis (Fig. 4B). NCB showed a shared pattern across CD4 TEM, Treg, and CXCL13+ cells, whereas CB displayed a specific, independent pattern in the Treg, indicating divergent regulatory inputs. A Venn survey of genes defining the CD4 TEM signaling pattern identified 33 common signals, including CD86, nectin, ICAM, PVR, and galectin (Fig. 4C). CellChat inference demonstrated reduced quantity and strength of CD86, ICAM, and galectin interactions in CB compared with NCB (Fig. 4D). Ligand mapping placed ICAM1/ICAM2, galectin-9 (LGALS9), and CD86 predominantly in cDC2 and CXCL10+ macrophages, mirroring the NECTIN2 expression pattern, whereas receptor mapping showed CTLA4 and CD28 enriched in Treg and ITGAL and CD44 in CD4 TEM (Fig. 4E and F). Consistent with these networks, Treg canonical surface markers revealed that CTLA4 decreased from BL to OT in CB, whereas both TIGIT and CTLA4 increased in NCB (Fig. 4G). In NCB, ICAM/galectin cues from cDC2 and CXCL10+ macrophages likely recruit CD4 TEM cells into the TME (27–29) (consistent with the adhesion-dependent spreading pathway in Fig. 3F) and, via CTLA4 activation, promote their conversion into suppressive Treg, thereby sustaining immunosuppression. In CB, preexisting Treg adopt a less-suppressive program and are not replenished from the TEM pool under treatment. Thus, differences in clinical outcome may reflect relief of BL Treg dominance in CB versus de novo Treg induction in NCB. Thus, CTLA4 blockade may be a potential combination to overcome resistance to the combination.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, the combination of SBRT followed by atezolizumab plus tiragolumab showed a median PFS of 9.3 months in treatment-naïve NSCLC. Atezolizumab plus tiragolumab in a PD-L1–selected (TPS ≥ 1%) population showed a median PFS of 5.4 months (12). Although our study cannot be directly compared with the previous trials, and cross-trial comparison should be interpreted with caution due to different patient populations, the addition of SBRT combined with atezolizumab plus tiragolumab showed an improvement in PFS.

These findings may be both attributable to the relatively indolent nature of oligometastatic disease as well as the role of SBRT in priming immune cells to recognize a wider range of tumor-associated antigens (30). Previous reports of pembrolizumab after completion of SBRT showed a median PFS of 19.1 months in patients with oligometastatic NSCLC with ≤ 4 metastatic sites, and PD-L1 expression was not associated with the magnitude of PFS benefit (9). Our study included up to 10 metastatic sites that were all irradiated with SBRT and included various metastatic sites, including the bone, lung, brain, and liver.

Currently, the standard of care for advanced NSCLC without driver alteration depends on the PD-L1 expression. For patients with high PD-L1 expression, defined as TPS of 50% or more, PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors as monotherapy are sufficient to derive clinical benefit, whereas those with TPS 0% to 49% require the addition of chemotherapy. Recently, novel therapeutic approaches such as ivonescimab, a bispecific antibody targeting PD-1 and VEGF, showed PFS benefit in PD-L1–positive NSCLC (3). Novel therapeutic agents such as antibody–drug conjugates are combined with chemotherapy and immunotherapy, and the treatment paradigm continuously evolves in treatment-naïve advanced NSCLC.

Although the phase II CITYSCAPE study of atezolizumab with tiragolumab in PD-L1–positive NSCLC initially showed clinically meaningful improvement in ORR and PFS (12), atezolizumab plus tiragolumab failed to meet OS benefit in the PD-L1–high population in the SKYSCRAPER-01 study (13). In addition, atezolizumab plus tiragolumab did not demonstrate improvement in PFS over durvalumab in unresectable stage III NSCLC without progression after definitive platinum-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy in the SKYSCRAPER-03 study (31).

Previous studies have proposed that TIGIT primarily exerts immunosuppressive activity by attenuating CD226-mediated costimulation or by modulating DC function (32, 33). The NECTIN2–TIGIT axis constitutes an important inhibitory pathway that actively contributes to immune suppression within the TME (34, 35). However, these investigations did not resolve how TIGIT blockade reshapes the hierarchical organization of CD8+ T-cell states. In contrast, our study delineates distinct immune trajectories that explain the divergent outcomes observed following SBRT combined with tiragolumab and atezolizumab. In responders, therapeutic inhibition of the NECTIN–TIGIT axis selectively amplified the activation and proliferative expansion of CD8+ TEX and TPEX populations. The coordinated reinforcement of exhaustion–progenitor and cytotoxic programs seemed to potentiate adaptive antitumor immunity and support durable clinical benefit. Responders likewise exhibited attenuation of baseline Treg dominance and a shift toward a more balanced CD4+ helper T-cell milieu, suggesting that effective TIGIT blockade may recalibrate the equilibrium between regulatory and effector immunity within the TME.

Treg can preserve suppressive dominance through compensatory mechanisms. For example, continuous TCR signaling has been shown to maintain a functional Treg pool (36), whereas additional studies have highlighted that Treg identity and suppressive function are stabilized by epigenetic programs that allow them to adapt to changes within the immune microenvironment (37). Moreover, the distinctive metabolic constraints of the TME selectively support Treg survival and suppressive activity, thereby reinforcing the persistence of Treg-mediated immunoregulation (38). However, these investigations did not identify the upstream molecular cues or T-cell populations that initiate compensatory Treg expansion following checkpoint perturbation.

Our study addresses this gap by demonstrating that ICAM- and galectin-dependent recruitment of CD4+ TEM cells serves as the upstream driver promoting the emergence of newly generated CTLA4high T cells. This defines a mechanistic compensatory T-cell axis not previously described in the TIGIT-focused literature. These findings indicate that targeting the NECTIN–TIGIT axis alone may be insufficient to dismantle the Treg circuitry in certain tumors and highlight CTLA4 signaling as a dominant compensatory pathway mobilized following TIGIT blockade.

Collectively, our results support a model in which dual modulation of inhibitory networks—via TIGIT inhibition to amplify CD8+ TEX/TPEX immunity and CTLA4 blockade to restrain compensatory Treg expansion—may represent a rational combinatorial strategy to overcome primary resistance. By revealing that therapeutic efficacy depends on simultaneously enhancing TEX/TPEX immunity and limiting CTLA4high Treg compensation, our study expands the mechanistic framework for understanding TIGIT-targeted therapies and identifies regulatory pathways that may be leveraged to improve their effectiveness.

This study has several limitations. The sample size and heterogeneity of clinical specimens may limit the broader applicability of our findings. In particular, as our samples were derived from different anatomic sites, baseline tissue-specific immune features may have contributed to intersample variability. Nevertheless, prior studies have shown that clinical scRNA-seq datasets from heterogeneous anatomic sources can be successfully integrated to extract biologically meaningful insights into immune microenvironmental states (39, 40). Consistent with this framework, our analyses focused on relative intratumoral immune changes associated with treatment rather than absolute organ-specific differences. In addition, we identified ICAM/galectin-mediated recruitment of CD4+ TEM cells and the emergence of CTLA4high Treg in nonresponders, although these mechanistic observations require further experimental validation. Finally, although our data support the rationale for combining TIGIT and CTLA4 blockade, the clinical efficacy and safety of such therapeutic strategies must be assessed in future prospective studies.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In treatment-naïve NSCLC without driver alterations, SBRT followed by atezolizumab showed meaningful clinical activity, and our data indicate that therapeutic efficacy depends on amplifying CD8+ TEX/TPEX immunity while restraining compensatory CTLA4high Treg expansion. These insights could support combined TIGIT and CTLA4 blockade as a rational strategy to overcome primary resistance.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The scRNA-seq data are not publicly available due to patient privacy considerations but are available upon reasonable request by contacting the corresponding author, in accordance with applicable regulations. All other raw and processed data supporting the findings of this study, including those underlying the figures, are also available upon request. Code availability: All original code for scRNA-seq analyses has been deposited at GitHub and are publicly available at https://github.com/SanghoonLee-1/SkyRocket.git as of the date of publication.
